results.title: Random forest and spatial cross-validation performance in predicting species abundance distributions | Environmental Systems Research
results.content: We used the standard RF to test the influence of three sampling methods on the predictive performance of five spatial CV and the standard 5-fold CV strategies in modelling species abundance distribution accounting for species features (abundance class and detection probability) and data features (sample size and spatial autocorrelation variation strength). For high spatially autocorrelated abundance data, the analysis suggests that when the sampling is systematic or random the spatial K-fold CV with a checkerboard pattern in the assignment of blocks to folds yields expected population \(R^2\) but it is not significantly different to other CV methods, except environmental blocking and buffered leave-one-out CV which underestimates the RF predictive power for both rare and common species. The findings indicate that even in the presence of high spatial autocorrelation and imperfect detection, design-based validation and the standard K-fold CV remain effective strategies for evaluating the performance of machine learning methods for predicting species abundance, provided that sampling is random and, in some cases, systematic.

results.title: Do we need a testing set? - Questions - PyMC Discourse
results.content: I was listening to @ericmjl talk from PyData An Attempt At Demystifying Bayesian Deep Learning (really loved the talk by the way!) and he mentioned at the end during the comments that in a beyasian setting, we don’t need a testing set. If I want to use my model to predict data, how could I evaluate how good my model is if I don’t test its performance on unseen data? My impression of what Eric means is that Bayesian model does not overfit, so you don’t need a testing set to evaluate overfitting problem. But what you are essentially saying is that we don’t really need a validation set here because the model won’t really overfit the data? Are the stats we can calculate from our traces like , , , , can be used to evaluate the performance a model on unseen data? In that regards, `` might be the best metric, since it approximates the leave-one-out cross-validation score of your model. But ultimately, the model performance should be evaluated by whether it can predict future data. When we’re evaluating a model, we’re asking two questions, sequentially:. 1. Are we certain about the model? 2. Given that we are certain about the model, are we certain about the parameter values? With deep nets, we sort of throw out the first question - since deep nets can approximate any function, we don’t worry about the model specification. If we hold out data, then we just give less data to the model, and so we’ll be just less certain about parameter values. Thus, where I was going with that train/test split comment was that conditioned on the model being correct (or being black box), we don’t need train/test splits in a Bayesian setting. Use as many methods as you can to justify the model structure - train/test split, argumentation with/learning from subject matter experts, information criterion, leave-one-out CV. That’s the more important step in the modeling process, and IMHO, given the complexity of the world and the approximate nature of our models, **there shouldn’t be “one and preferably only one way” to evaluate how good our model is**.

results.title: Cross-Validation in Machine Learning: The Ultimate Guide to Model ...
results.content: Cross-Validation in Machine Learning: The Ultimate Guide to Model Evaluation - Tech Learn with Data #### Data Science, Data Engineering, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, LLM, Time Series, ML Ops Cross-Validation in Machine Learning: The Ultimate Guide to Model Evaluation Date: January 7, 2025Author: Navin Malik 0 Comments Building a machine learning model is exciting, but how do you know if it’s any good? In this guide, we’ll explore what cross-validation is, why it’s essential, and how to use it effectively to make your machine learning models robust. ### **What is Cross-Validation?** Cross-validation is a resampling technique used to evaluate the performance of a machine learning model. It splits your dataset into multiple subsets, trains the model on some of them, and tests it on the remaining ones. ### **Why is Cross-Validation Important?** Cross-validation helps ensure that your model isn’t just memorizing the training data but can perform well on new, unseen data. Instead of relying on a single train-test split, cross-validation averages results across multiple splits, giving you a more accurate estimate of model performance. 3. **Works with Limited Data** When you don’t have a lot of data, cross-validation makes the most of it by reusing the same data for training and testing. **Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV)** Uses one data point as the test set and the rest as the training set. ### **How to Implement Cross-Validation in Python** Here’s how to perform K-Fold Cross-Validation using scikit-learn: from sklearn.model\_selection import cross\_val\_score from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.datasets import load\_iris # Load dataset X, y = data.data, data.target # Initialize model # Perform 5-Fold Cross-Validation cv\_scores = cross\_val\_score(model, X, y, cv=5) print("Cross-Validation Scores:", cv\_scores) print("Mean CV Score:", cv\_scores.mean()) ### **For Stratified K-Fold:** from sklearn.model\_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross\_val\_score skf = StratifiedKFold(n\_splits=5) cv\_scores = cross\_val\_score(model, X, y, cv=skf) print("Stratified CV Scores:", cv\_scores) ### **When to Use Cross-Validation** * **Model Evaluation:** Use CV to assess how well your model will generalize to unseen data. Whether you’re working with a small dataset or a complex deep learning model, cross-validation is your best friend for reliable model evaluation. So, the next time you’re tempted to train-test split and call it a day, think about cross-validation—it’s the extra effort that separates a good model from a great one!
